title: Async & concurrency for many model calls
summary: Learn async and await in Python so your code can wait on many LLM calls at once instead of one at a time, using asyncio.gather to fan out dozens of requests concurrently.
objectives: Explain why LLM calls are I/O-bound and how that makes concurrency a huge win
Define an async function and call it with await
Use asyncio.gather to run many model calls concurrently and collect all results
Use the AsyncAnthropic client to make non-blocking Messages API calls
Bound concurrency with a semaphore so you respect rate limits
Recognise when to reach for threads or processes instead of asyncio

quiz.q: Why does concurrency help so much when making many LLM calls?
options: LLM calls are CPU-bound, so more cores finish faster
LLM calls are I/O-bound: most of the time is spent waiting on the network, so you can wait on many at once
It reduces the number of tokens billed
It makes each individual response shorter
quiz.why: An LLM call spends almost all its time waiting for the model's response over the network, so while one waits another can start — that overlap is where concurrency pays off.

options: Runs coroutines one after another in order
Schedules many coroutines to run concurrently and returns all their results together
Converts a function into a thread
Caches the results of a coroutine
quiz.why: asyncio.gather takes multiple awaitables, runs them concurrently on the event loop, and returns a list of their results once all have finished.

quiz.q: What keyword pauses a coroutine until an awaitable result is ready?
quiz.why: await suspends the coroutine and hands control back to the event loop until the awaited operation completes, letting other coroutines run meanwhile.

quiz.q: Why bound concurrency with an asyncio.Semaphore when calling an LLM API?
options: It makes responses arrive in order
It limits how many requests are in flight at once so you stay under the provider's rate limits
It is required for await to work
quiz.why: Firing thousands of requests at once will trip rate limits; a semaphore caps the number of simultaneous in-flight calls to a safe ceiling.

quiz.q: In one sentence, what is the difference between async I/O and threads for this work?
quiz.answer: Async I/O uses a single thread and an event loop to interleave many waiting operations, which is ideal for I/O-bound work like network calls, whereas threads or processes are better for CPU-bound work.
quiz.why: asyncio shines when the bottleneck is waiting on the network; CPU-heavy work needs real parallelism from threads or processes.

quiz.q: What does an async function return when you call it without awaiting it?
quiz.answer: A coroutine object that has not run yet; you must await it or pass it to something like asyncio.gather to actually execute it.
quiz.why: Calling an async function only creates a coroutine — the event loop runs it when you await it or schedule it as a task.

body_markdown:
## Why concurrency matters for LLM work

Most of your automation so far probably ran one step, then the next, then the next. That is fine when each step is quick. But an LLM call is different: you send a request and then **wait** — often a second or several — for the model to think and stream back tokens. The work isn't your CPU; it's the network and the model far away. We call this **I/O-bound** work.

Now imagine you need to summarise 200 documents, or classify a backlog of 5,000 support tickets. Done one at a time, you pay the full wait for every single call and the total time is brutal. The insight is simple: while one call is waiting, your program could start another. That overlap is **concurrency**, and for many LLM calls it can turn an hour into a minute.

## async and await in one breath

Python's tool for this is `asyncio`. You mark a function `async def`, which makes it a **coroutine**. Inside it, wherever you'd normally block waiting on something, you write `await`. The `await` keyword suspends that coroutine and hands control back to an **event loop**, which is free to run other coroutines while the first one waits.

```python
import asyncio

async def greet(name):
    await asyncio.sleep(1)   # pretend this is a network call
    return f"Hello, {name}"

async def main():
    print(await greet("Kwasi"))

asyncio.run(main())
```

Calling `greet("Kwasi")` on its own does **not** run it — it returns a coroutine object. It only runs when you `await` it, or hand it to the event loop. `asyncio.run(main())` starts the loop and runs your top-level coroutine.

## Fanning out with asyncio.gather

The payoff is `asyncio.gather`. Give it many coroutines and it runs them **concurrently**, returning all results once they finish.

```python
import asyncio
from anthropic import AsyncAnthropic

client = AsyncAnthropic()

async def classify(ticket):
    msg = await client.messages.create(
        model="claude-haiku-4-5-20251001",
        max_tokens=50,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": f"Label this ticket: {ticket}"}],
    )
    return msg.content[0].text

async def main(tickets):
    results = await asyncio.gather(*(classify(t) for t in tickets))
    return results

asyncio.run(main(my_tickets))
```

Note `AsyncAnthropic` and `await client.messages.create(...)`: the SDK gives you a non-blocking client so the call cooperates with the event loop. The same idea applies on Amazon Bedrock or Azure with their async clients.

## Respecting rate limits with a semaphore

Fanning out 5,000 calls at once will trip the provider's **rate limits** and get you HTTP 429s. Bound the concurrency with an `asyncio.Semaphore` so only, say, 10 calls are in flight at a time.

```python
sem = asyncio.Semaphore(10)

async def classify(ticket):
    async with sem:
        msg = await client.messages.create(...)
        return msg.content[0].text
```

The `async with sem` acquires a slot before the call and releases it after, capping in-flight work at a safe ceiling — much like limiting parallel jobs in a CI/CD pipeline.

## When asyncio is the wrong tool

asyncio is for **I/O-bound** work — waiting on networks, disks, APIs. If your bottleneck is heavy computation (CPU-bound), a single event loop won't help; reach for `concurrent.futures` with threads or, for true parallelism, processes. For calling LLMs, though, async is almost always exactly right.

## Your task

Write an async script that takes a list of 20 short prompts, calls a Claude model for each one concurrently with `asyncio.gather`, bounds concurrency to 5 with a semaphore, and prints all the answers. Time it against a plain sequential loop and note the difference.

slides.narration: Welcome to Module Five, where your automation-style Python grows into application engineering. We start with one of the highest-leverage skills for a GenAI engineer: concurrency. When you need to make many model calls, doing them one at a time is painfully slow. In this lesson you'll learn async and await, and how to fan out dozens of calls at once so an hour of work finishes in a minute.

slides.title: LLM calls are I/O-bound
bullets: You send a request, then wait on the network.
The wait dominates — not your CPU.
While one call waits, another could start.
That overlap is concurrency.
slides.narration: Here's the key insight. When you call a language model, you send a request and then wait, often a second or several, for the answer to come back over the network. Your processor is mostly idle during that wait. We call this I O bound work. And the moment you realise that, a door opens: while one call is sitting there waiting, your program could already be starting the next one. That overlap is what we mean by concurrency.

slides.title: Why this matters at scale
bullets: Summarise 200 documents. Classify 5,000 tickets.
One at a time, you pay every wait in full.
Concurrent, the waits overlap.
Hours can become minutes.
slides.narration: Picture a real job: summarise two hundred documents, or classify a backlog of five thousand support tickets. Done strictly one at a time, you pay the full waiting time for every single call, and the total is brutal. Run them concurrently and all those waits overlap. The same workload that took an hour can finish in a minute. This is why concurrency is one of the first production skills a GenAI engineer needs.

slides.title: async and await
bullets: async def makes a coroutine.
await pauses it and frees the event loop.
Calling a coroutine doesn't run it — awaiting does.
asyncio.run starts the loop.
slides.code:
import asyncio

async def greet(name):
    await asyncio.sleep(1)
    return f"Hello, {name}"

asyncio.run(greet("Kwasi"))
slides.narration: Python's tool for this is asyncio. You mark a function with async def, which makes it a coroutine. Inside, wherever you'd normally block waiting on something, you write await. That await keyword pauses the coroutine and hands control back to the event loop, which is then free to run other coroutines. One thing that surprises people: just calling an async function does not run it. It returns a coroutine object. It only runs when you await it, or hand it to the loop with asyncio dot run.

slides.title: Fan out with asyncio.gather
bullets: Give gather many coroutines.
It runs them concurrently.
Returns all results when they finish.
One line replaces a slow loop.
slides.narration: The real payoff is asyncio dot gather. You hand it many coroutines and it schedules them all to run concurrently on the event loop, then returns a list of every result once they've all finished. So instead of a slow loop that does one ticket, waits, then the next, you write one line that launches them all at once and collects the answers. This single function is the workhorse of concurrent LLM code.

slides.title: Non-blocking Anthropic calls
bullets: Use AsyncAnthropic, not Anthropic.
await client.messages.create(...).
The call cooperates with the event loop.
Same pattern on Bedrock and Azure.
slides.code:
from anthropic import AsyncAnthropic
client = AsyncAnthropic()

msg = await client.messages.create(
    model="claude-haiku-4-5-20251001",
    max_tokens=50,
    messages=[{"role": "user",
               "content": ticket}],
)
slides.narration: To make this work with Claude, you use the async client, AsyncAnthropic, and you await client dot messages dot create. That gives you a non-blocking call that cooperates with the event loop instead of freezing it. We're using a Haiku model here because for high-volume classification you want the fastest, cheapest model that's good enough. The same async pattern applies on Amazon Bedrock and Azure with their own async clients, so this skill travels with you across clouds.

slides.title: Bound it with a semaphore
bullets: Thousands of calls at once trips rate limits.
asyncio.Semaphore caps in-flight calls.
async with sem around each call.
Like limiting parallel CI jobs.
slides.code:
sem = asyncio.Semaphore(10)

async def classify(ticket):
    async with sem:
        msg = await client.messages.create(...)
        return msg.content[0].text
slides.narration: There's a trap waiting for you. If you fan out five thousand calls at literally the same instant, you'll slam into the provider's rate limits and get a wall of four-two-nine errors. The fix is a semaphore. An asyncio dot Semaphore lets you cap how many calls are in flight at once, say ten. You wrap each call in async with sem, which grabs a slot before the call and releases it after. If you've ever limited the number of parallel jobs in a CI pipeline, this is exactly that idea.

slides.title: When NOT to use asyncio
bullets: asyncio is for I/O-bound work.
CPU-heavy work won't speed up on one loop.
For computation: threads or processes.
For LLM calls: async is almost always right.
slides.narration: One honest caveat. asyncio is built for I O bound work, things that spend their time waiting on networks, disks, or APIs. If your real bottleneck is heavy computation, crunching numbers, a single event loop won't help you, because the loop runs on one thread. For that you'd reach for the concurrent dot futures module with threads, or processes for true parallelism. But for the work in front of you, calling language models, async is almost always exactly the right tool.

bullets: LLM calls are I/O-bound — concurrency wins big.
async def + await + an event loop.
asyncio.gather fans out many calls.
A semaphore keeps you under rate limits.

slides.narration: Let's recap. LLM calls are I O bound, which is exactly why concurrency gives you such a huge win. You write coroutines with async def, pause them with await, and the event loop interleaves the waiting. asyncio dot gather fans out many calls at once, and a semaphore keeps you safely under the rate limits.
